title: Nullability
summary: Say which values may be missing, and let the compiler catch the crash before it happens.

steps.title: null means nothing is there
body: A variable of a class type holds a reference to an object. It can also hold `null`: a reference to **nothing**.
That is useful. A customer may have no middle name. A search may find no match. `null` says so.
The trouble starts when code forgets to ask:
```csharp
string? middleName = null;
Console.WriteLine(middleName.Length);   // crashes
```text
Unhandled exception. System.NullReferenceException:
Object reference not set to an instance of an object.
There is no object, so there is no `Length` to read. `NullReferenceException` is one of the most common crashes in real software, and it usually shows up far from the line that caused it.
The rest of this lesson is about making it the compiler's problem instead of your customer's.

options: It prints `Checking code...` and then crashes with a `NullReferenceException`
It prints `Checking code...` and then an empty line
steps.explain: It compiles, with a warning. The first line runs fine. The crash comes at the moment the program tries to call a method on nothing.

steps.title: string and string?
body: C# lets you write down whether a reference may be null:
- `string name` promises: **never null**.
- `string? middleName` admits: **might be null**.
The compiler then checks your promises and **warns** you. You will see these warnings under the editor when you run code.
```csharp
string? middleName = FindMiddleName();
Console.WriteLine(middleName.Length);        // warning: may be null here
if (middleName != null)
Console.WriteLine(middleName.Length);    // fine: you checked
The compiler follows the flow of your code. Inside the `if`, it knows `middleName` cannot be null, so the warning disappears.
It also warns the other way round: putting `null`, or a `string?`, into a plain `string` breaks the promise.
> **Tip:** Treat these warnings as errors. Each one is a crash that has not happened yet.

steps.prompt: Given `string first = "Maya";` and `string? middle = FindMiddleName();`, which lines make the compiler warn?
steps.explain: A warning appears when a maybe-null value is used as if it were definitely there, or when null is put where it was promised never to be. Going from *never null* to *maybe null* is always safe.

steps.title: Three operators for missing values
body: Writing `if (x != null)` everywhere gets noisy. Three operators do the common cases in one go.
**`?.` only go on if there is something there.** If the left side is null, the whole expression is null instead of crashing.
```csharp
int? length = middleName?.Length;   // null when middleName is null
**`??` use this instead when it is null.**
```csharp
string shown = middleName ?? "(none)";
**`??=` fill it in only if it is null.**
```csharp
middleName ??= "(none)";   // assigns only when middleName is null
They chain well: `middleName?.Length ?? 0` reads as *the length, or 0 if there is no middle name*.

steps.explain: `??` supplies a fallback. `?.` reads `Length` only when there is a string. `??=` fills in `nickname` because it was null, and leaves `city` alone because it was not.

steps.prompt: Match each piece of syntax to what it does.
pairs: declares that the value may be null
reads the member, or gives null when `a` is null
stores `b` in `a` only when `a` is null
a check the compiler remembers afterwards

steps.title: The missing company
prompt: Both methods take a `company` that may be missing, and both crash when it is. Run the code and read the **warnings**: the compiler has already found the two problem lines.
- `ShippingLabel("Maya", " Acme ")` should return `"Maya, Acme"`
- `ShippingLabel("Maya", null)` should return `"Maya"`
- `CompanyLength("Acme")` should return `4`
- `CompanyLength(null)` should return `0`
Fix them so they work for both cases and the warnings are gone.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("ShippingLabel(\"Maya\", \" Acme \") trims and joins", "Maya, Acme", ShippingLabel("Maya", " Acme "));
Dojo.Try("ShippingLabel(\"Maya\", null) returns just the name", () => Dojo.Eq("ShippingLabel(\"Maya\", null) returns just the name", "Maya", ShippingLabel("Maya", null)));
Dojo.Eq("CompanyLength(\"Acme\") returns 4", 4, CompanyLength("Acme"));
Dojo.Try("CompanyLength(null) returns 0", () => Dojo.Eq("CompanyLength(null) returns 0", 0, CompanyLength(null)));

forbid.message: Does not silence the warning with `!.`

hints: In `ShippingLabel`, decide what to return when `company == null` before the line that uses it.
`CompanyLength` is one expression: read the length only if there is a company, otherwise use 0.

steps.title: Nullable numbers, and the ! escape hatch
body: An `int` always has a value, so it cannot say *unknown*. Using 0 or -1 to mean *missing* is a trap: is that customer zero years old, or did nobody ask?
Add `?` to a value type and it can hold null as well:
```csharp
int? age = null;
Console.WriteLine(age.HasValue);   // False
Console.WriteLine(age ?? 0);       // 0
age = 34;
Console.WriteLine(age.Value);      // 34
`HasValue` asks whether a number is there. `Value` reads it, and **throws** if there is none, so check first or use `??`.
One more operator, to be used sparingly. `!` after an expression tells the compiler *trust me, this is not null*:
```csharp
Console.WriteLine(middleName!.Length);
It removes the warning and does **nothing else**. If you are wrong, the program crashes exactly as before. Reach for a check or `??` first.

steps.explain: A missing discount falls back to 0. Comparing null with `>` is simply false: *unknown* is not greater than 10.

steps.prompt: Get the length of a promo code that may be missing (0 if there is none), then give it a default.
steps.explain: `?.` avoids the crash, `??` supplies the fallback, and `??=` assigns only when the variable is still null.

steps.title: An address book with gaps
prompt: Real contact data has holes. Model them honestly.
**`Contact`**
- constructor `Contact(string name, string? email, int? age)`
- `get`-only properties `Name` (`string`), `Email` (`string?`), `Age` (`int?`)
**`AddressBook`**
- `void Add(Contact contact)`
- `Contact? Find(string name)`: the contact with that name, or `null`
- `string EmailOf(string name)`: the contact's email, or `"unknown"` when the contact does not exist **or** has no email
- `bool IsAdult(string name)`: `true` only when the contact exists and has a known age of 18 or more
- `int TotalKnownAge()`: the sum of the ages that are known
Aim for zero warnings and no `!`.
starter: // Email and Age may be missing
public Contact(string name, string? email, int? age)
private readonly Dictionary<string, Contact> _contacts = new Dictionary<string, Contact>();
solution: public Contact(string name, string? email, int? age)
private readonly Dictionary<string, Contact> _contacts = new Dictionary<string, Contact>();
template: var dojoMaya = new Contact("Maya", "maya@example.com", 34);
var dojoBen = new Contact("Ben", null, 16);
var dojoCy = new Contact("Cy", "cy@example.com", null);
Dojo.Eq<string?>("Contact stores an email", "maya@example.com", dojoMaya.Email);
Dojo.Eq<string?>("Contact stores a missing email as null", null, dojoBen.Email);
Dojo.Eq<int?>("Contact stores an age", 34, dojoMaya.Age);
Dojo.Eq<int?>("Contact stores a missing age as null", null, dojoCy.Age);
var dojoBook = new AddressBook();
dojoBook.Add(dojoMaya);
dojoBook.Add(dojoBen);
dojoBook.Add(dojoCy);
Dojo.Check("Find(\"Maya\") returns Maya's contact", ReferenceEquals(dojoBook.Find("Maya"), dojoMaya), "Expected the same Contact object that was added");
Dojo.Check("Find(\"Nobody\") returns null", dojoBook.Find("Nobody") == null, "Expected null for a name that was never added");
Dojo.Try("EmailOf(\"Maya\") returns her email", () => Dojo.Eq("EmailOf(\"Maya\") returns her email", "maya@example.com", dojoBook.EmailOf("Maya")));
Dojo.Try("EmailOf(\"Ben\") is unknown: he has no email", () => Dojo.Eq("EmailOf(\"Ben\") is unknown: he has no email", "unknown", dojoBook.EmailOf("Ben")));
Dojo.Try("EmailOf(\"Nobody\") is unknown: no such contact", () => Dojo.Eq("EmailOf(\"Nobody\") is unknown: no such contact", "unknown", dojoBook.EmailOf("Nobody")));
Dojo.Try("IsAdult(\"Maya\") is true (34)", () => Dojo.Eq("IsAdult(\"Maya\") is true (34)", true, dojoBook.IsAdult("Maya")));
Dojo.Try("IsAdult(\"Ben\") is false (16)", () => Dojo.Eq("IsAdult(\"Ben\") is false (16)", false, dojoBook.IsAdult("Ben")));
Dojo.Try("IsAdult(\"Cy\") is false: age unknown", () => Dojo.Eq("IsAdult(\"Cy\") is false: age unknown", false, dojoBook.IsAdult("Cy")));
Dojo.Try("IsAdult(\"Nobody\") is false: no such contact", () => Dojo.Eq("IsAdult(\"Nobody\") is false: no such contact", false, dojoBook.IsAdult("Nobody")));
Dojo.Try("TotalKnownAge() is 50 (34 + 16, Cy skipped)", () => Dojo.Eq("TotalKnownAge() is 50 (34 + 16, Cy skipped)", 50, dojoBook.TotalKnownAge()));
{{CODE}}
hints: `Find` uses `ContainsKey`, as in the inventory exercise, and ends with `return null;`. Its return type `Contact?` is what makes that honest.
`EmailOf` has two things that may be missing, the contact and the email. One chain handles both: `Find(name)?.Email ?? "unknown"`.
`Find(name)?.Age >= 18` is already `false` when either part is null. In `TotalKnownAge`, add `contact.Age ?? 0` for each contact in `_contacts.Values`.

steps.title: Sidekick: a TaskItem that is honest about gaps
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk add "Fix login" --tag bug --project web` needs a task that can have a tag, a project and a
due date, or not. Today your `TaskItem` (from *Constructors and properties*) has no way to say "no due date". Add it
honestly, with nullable types, so the compiler makes every caller check.
Start from your `TaskItem` (it is in the editor) and keep everything it does. Add:
- `public string? Tag { get; set; }`: the setter **normalises**: `null`, `""` or only spaces store `null`;
anything else is trimmed and lower-cased (`"  Auth "` → `"auth"`). Use a private `string? tag` field.
- `public string? Project { get; set; }` and `public DateOnly? Due { get; set; }`: plain auto-properties.
- `public string Label()`: the title, then ` [tag]` if there is a tag, ` @project` if the project is not null or
empty, and ` (due Mon 30 Nov)` if there is a due date (format `ddd d MMM`).
```text
new TaskItem(1, "Fix login")                              Label() -> Fix login
Tag = "Bug", Project = "web", Due = 2026-11-30            Label() -> Fix login [bug] @web (due Mon 30 Nov)
Project = ""                                              Label() -> Fix login   (empty counts as missing)
> **Tip:** `Project is { Length: > 0 } p` is true only for a non-null, non-empty string, and hands you `p`.
starter: public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
solution: public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
hints: The setter: `set => tag = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value) ? null : value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();`
In `Label()` build three parts, each `""` when the value is missing: `Tag is null ? "" : $" [{Tag}]"`.
For the date: `Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : ""`.
template: var dojoTask = new TaskItem(1, "Fix login");
Dojo.Eq<string?>("a new task has no tag", null, dojoTask.Tag);
Dojo.Eq<string?>("a new task has no project", null, dojoTask.Project);
Dojo.Eq<DateOnly?>("a new task has no due date", null, dojoTask.Due);
Dojo.Eq("Label() of a bare task is its title", "Fix login", dojoTask.Label());
dojoTask.Tag = "  Auth ";
Dojo.Eq<string?>("Tag \"  Auth \" is stored as \"auth\"", "auth", dojoTask.Tag);
dojoTask.Tag = "   ";
Dojo.Eq<string?>("a blank tag is stored as null", null, dojoTask.Tag);
dojoTask.Tag = "Bug";
dojoTask.Project = "web";
dojoTask.Due = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30);
Dojo.Eq("Label() with tag, project and due date", "Fix login [bug] @web (due Mon 30 Nov)", dojoTask.Label());
dojoTask.Tag = null;
dojoTask.Project = "";
Dojo.Eq("an empty project and a null tag are left out", "Fix login (due Mon 30 Nov)", dojoTask.Label());
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("a blank title is still refused", () => new TaskItem(2, "  "));
var dojoTimed = new TaskItem(3, "Write tests", 30);
dojoTimed.Start(new DateTime(2026, 11, 25, 9, 0, 0));
dojoTimed.Stop(new DateTime(2026, 11, 25, 9, 40, 0));
Dojo.Eq("the timer still logs minutes", 40, dojoTimed.LoggedMinutes);
Dojo.Eq("the estimate is still kept", 30, dojoTimed.EstimateMinutes);
{{CODE}}
steps.explain: A `string?` property tells every caller "this may be missing". The compiler then warns wherever someone uses it without checking, which is exactly the bug class you want gone. Normalising in the setter means the rest of Sidekick never has to wonder whether `" "` counts as a tag.

build.title: TaskItem with honest optional fields
build.unlocks: Your tasks can now carry a tag, a project and a due date: `sk add "Fix login" --tag bug`.
